review.notes: Built on the course: charter, roles, WBS and 100% rule, scope creep, CPM and float, crashing vs fast tracking, parametric estimate, reserves, EVM (CPI, SPI, EAC), risk vs issue, P x I, threat responses. All calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Coastline Foods (fictional), a food manufacturer building new warehouse racking
content.briefing: You manage a project to install new racking in the finished-goods warehouse. Budget: Kz 10 million. Target: 9 weeks. The operations director is the sponsor. The warehouse must keep shipping during the work.

variants.text: The sponsor wants to start work tomorrow 'and write things down later'. What do you do first?

choices.t: Agree a short charter: purpose, objectives, scope, budget, top risks
choices.f: One page, signed in two days. Later arguments about scope are settled by it.

choices.t: Start tomorrow and document decisions as the work goes on
choices.f: Without a charter, nobody agrees what 'done' means. Disputes start in week 2.

choices.t: Write a full 40-page plan before any work starts at all
choices.f: Planning is needed, but a charter comes first and the details follow.

variants.text: Which objective is fit for the charter?

choices.t: Install 1,200 pallet positions by 30 June within Kz 10 million
choices.f: SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and timed.

choices.t: Greatly improve warehouse storage capacity as soon as possible
choices.f: Not measurable or timed. Nobody can say when it is achieved.

choices.t: Install new racking with the best quality and at the lowest cost
choices.f: A wish, not an objective. Add numbers and a date.

variants.text: Your WBS has racking, installation and safety inspection, but no project management or staff training. The sponsor approves it.

choices.t: Add the missing work: the WBS must hold 100% of it
choices.f: The 100% rule: all the work and only that work, including project management.

choices.t: Keep it; management and training are overhead, not work
choices.f: Unplanned work still costs time and money. The budget is short.

choices.t: Add them later if there is still budget left at the end
choices.f: Later means unfunded. Include them in the WBS now.

variants.text: A team member proposes one work package: 'install all racking', estimated at 900 hours.

choices.t: Split it by aisle, so each package is 8 to 80 hours
choices.f: Smaller packages have one owner, can be estimated and have a clear 'done'.

choices.t: Keep it as one package; it is one type of task
choices.f: 900 hours cannot be tracked or estimated well. Problems hide inside it.

choices.t: Split it into two packages of 450 hours each
choices.f: Still far too large to control. Aim for 8 to 80 hours.

variants.text: In week 3, the warehouse manager asks the installers to also paint the floor markings. It is not in scope.

choices.t: Log a change request with its impact on time and cost
choices.f: The sponsor approves it with 3 extra days and Kz 400,000. Scope stays controlled.

choices.t: Agree informally; it is small and keeps him happy
choices.f: Scope creep. Three more 'small' requests follow and the date slips.

choices.t: Refuse it outright; the scope is fixed once signed
choices.f: Firm, but the request may be valuable. Use change control, not a blanket no.

variants.text: An installer adds extra decorative end panels nobody asked for, 'to make it look premium'.

choices.t: Stop it: gold plating uses time and money
choices.f: Extras nobody asked for consume budget. Deliver what was agreed.

choices.t: Allow it; the customer will be pleased
choices.f: The panels cost Kz 600,000 that the budget does not have.

choices.t: Allow it if the team works extra hours
choices.f: Overtime still costs money, and the scope was never agreed.

variants.text: Your network has three paths: 6, 8 and 9 weeks. How long is the project, and where do you focus?

choices.t: 9 weeks; manage the 9-week path daily
choices.f: The longest path is critical. Any delay on it delays the end.

choices.t: 8 weeks; the average of the paths
choices.f: Durations are not averaged. The longest path sets the end.

choices.t: 6 weeks; the shortest path finishes first
choices.f: The project ends only when all paths are done: 9 weeks.

variants.text: Activity 'order racking' has early start week 3 and late start week 5. What is its total float?

choices.t: 2 weeks
choices.f: Correct: late start minus early start. It can slip 2 weeks without delaying the end.

choices.t: 0 weeks
choices.f: Zero float means critical. This activity has slack.

choices.t: 8 weeks
choices.f: You added the dates. Float = late start minus early start.

variants.text: The sponsor wants one week saved. Inspection must follow installation, which is on the critical path.

choices.t: Crash a critical task: add a second install crew
choices.f: Crashing adds resources at extra cost, on a critical activity. The week is saved.

choices.t: Add people to the non-critical labelling task
choices.f: That task has float. Speeding it up saves no time on the project.

choices.t: Overlap installation and safety inspection
choices.f: Fast tracking adds risk, and inspection must follow installation.

variants.text: Customs holds the racking at the port for 2 weeks. 'Receive racking' is critical. What happens?

choices.t: The end date moves 2 weeks unless you compress later work
choices.f: A delay on the critical path delays the project. You recalculate and plan options.

choices.t: Nothing; other tasks can use their float
choices.f: Float on other paths does not help a critical delay.

choices.t: It depends only on how fast installers work
choices.f: Faster installation can help, but first see that the end date moves.

variants.text: Racking costs Kz 15,000 per pallet position. You need 400 positions in aisle A. What is the parametric estimate?

choices.f: Correct: unit rate x quantity.
You added the numbers. Parametric = rate x quantity.
A zero is missing: 15,000 x 400 = 6,000,000.

variants.text: Estimates total Kz 9 million. You add Kz 600,000 for listed risks, and the board holds Kz 400,000 for the unknown. What is the cost baseline?

choices.t: Kz 9.6 million
choices.f: Correct: estimates + contingency. Management reserve is outside the baseline.

choices.t: Kz 10 million
choices.f: That includes management reserve. It is held by the board, not in the baseline.

choices.t: Kz 9 million
choices.f: Contingency for identified risks is part of the baseline.

variants.text: Week 4: PV = Kz 5.0 m, EV = Kz 4.0 m, AC = Kz 5.0 m. What are CPI and SPI?

choices.t: CPI 0.80, SPI 0.80: over budget and behind
choices.f: Correct: CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV. Both below 1.

choices.t: CPI 1.00, SPI 0.80: on budget but behind
choices.f: Spending equals plan, but you earned only Kz 4 m for Kz 5 m. Cost is a problem.

choices.t: CPI 1.25, SPI 1.25: under budget and ahead
choices.f: You divided the wrong way. CPI = EV / AC.

variants.text: Week 5: PV = Kz 4.0 m, EV = Kz 4.4 m, AC = Kz 4.0 m. What do you report?

choices.t: CPI 1.10, SPI 1.10: under budget and ahead
choices.f: Correct. Both indices above 1 are good.

choices.t: CPI 0.91, SPI 0.91: over budget and behind
choices.f: You divided the wrong way. CPI = EV / AC = 4.4 / 4.0.

choices.t: On plan, since actual cost equals planned value
choices.f: Comparing AC with PV mixes cost and time. Use EV.

variants.text: BAC is Kz 10 million and CPI is 0.80. If the trend continues, what is the estimate at completion?

choices.t: Kz 12.5 million
choices.f: Correct: EAC = BAC / CPI. You report the forecast and an action plan now.

choices.t: Kz 8.0 million
choices.f: You multiplied. A CPI below 1 means the final cost rises.

choices.t: Kz 10.0 million
choices.f: That assumes the problem disappears. Report the forecast, not hope.

variants.text: The CFO asks only 'how much have we spent?'. CPI is 0.85.

choices.t: Give spend and the forecast at completion
choices.f: Spend alone hides the overrun. The forecast lets the CFO act early.

choices.t: Give spend to date, which is what was asked
choices.f: Accurate, but the CFO learns of the overrun too late.

choices.t: Give spend and say the budget will be met
choices.f: With CPI 0.85, that is not true. Trust is lost when the overrun appears.

variants.text: Two risks: A, a crane delay (probability 4, impact 5). B, a paint shortage (probability 2, impact 3). Which first?

choices.t: A: score 20 against 6
choices.f: P x I: 4 x 5 = 20, 2 x 3 = 6. Focus on the highest score.

choices.t: B: it is easier to solve quickly
choices.f: Ease is not priority. The crane risk could stop the project.

choices.t: Both equally, in the order logged
choices.f: Logging order is not priority. Score them.

variants.text: The crane already broke down this morning. Where does it go?

choices.t: Issue log: it is happening now
choices.f: A risk is uncertain; an issue is already happening. You act today.

choices.t: Risk register, with a high score
choices.f: It is no longer uncertain. It needs action, not scoring.

choices.t: Nowhere; tell the sponsor by phone
choices.f: Tell the sponsor, yes, but log it so it is tracked and closed.

variants.text: Racking could be damaged in transport. You buy insurance. Which threat response is this?

choices.t: Transfer
choices.f: Correct: the financial impact passes to a third party.

choices.t: Avoid
choices.f: Avoid changes the plan to remove the risk. The risk still exists.

choices.t: Mitigate
choices.f: Mitigate reduces probability or impact, such as better packing.

variants.text: Installation work may block forklift lanes during shipping hours. What do you do?

choices.t: Avoid: install only at night when shipping stops
choices.f: Changing the plan removes the threat. Shipping is never blocked.

choices.t: Accept: the warehouse will cope somehow
choices.f: Shipping must continue. Accepting a high-impact threat is not reasonable.

choices.t: Transfer: ask the installer to pay any losses
choices.f: It moves cost, but late shipments still hurt customers.
